content.v: gather to select the Nobel Prize winners. The selection process is secret. All we know is that it usually takes months.
Toward the end of the process, four additional people are brought in: a writer, a translator, a project leader, and an

. That illustrator has been the same person for the past 14 years. His name is Johan Jarnestad. His job is to translate scientific ideas into drawings. The goal? To make complex science easy for the public to understand.

The 2023 Nobel Prize in Economics went to Claudia Goldin. The American economist discovered why men and women don’t always choose the same jobs or earn the same amount of money. In one of Jarnestad’s illustrations, three different generations of women stand on the same road. The first two are holding babies and looking back at their mothers. The last woman is looking back but also stepping forward with books in her hands. A sign at the end of the road points in two opposite directions. The backward direction is
“expectations”, and the forward “opportunities”. The picture looks simple, but it “clears up” Goldin’s complex findings. In the 20th century, the
between women and men hardly closed. This is because women decided how much and how hard they would study based on what their mothers did.

Jarnestad’s Nobel Prize illustrations all look different, but his drawing process is more or less the same. The artist attends meetings with the Nobel Committees. He draws and listens at the same time. Whenever he doesn’t understand something, he asks questions—lots of them. Later,
the drawing process, Jarnestad keeps asking himself: Is my understanding correct? Can the public understand my work? Does the drawing look nice? Does it catch people’s eye?
Jarnestad’s illustrations every year. She describes the drawings as an important communication tool. “They can’t stand on their own,” she says. “But the text wouldn’t work without them, either.”
